But with these two showing up together, that means it’s been five since the start.” "Trials run four survivors," he continued, looking around the group. "Four survivors, four generators, two gates. The whole thing's built around even numbers. So." He gestured vaguely at all of them. "Five." Nobody had a good answer for that. Dwight’s brows furrowed and he blinked slowly, the words catching something half-formed in his mind. He couldn’t quite place why, but something about it itched at him. Huffing lightly, he shook the feeling off. It was probably just the dark — the claustrophobia of it all. Orela had moved on to resume checking David's shoulder, unable to stay still in the silence anymore. David submitted to approximately four seconds of this before shifting away from her hands with an absent swat. "Stop it. I'm fine." "You're holding your arm like it's going to fall off." "It's not that bad. It’d feel better if you’d stop poking at it." Dwight watched the flashlight beam move around the room as Orela gestured, unwilling to lose track of the only light in the room. Every dip and bounce made his chest tighten. As she drifted around, fussing over an increasingly annoyed David, her steps disturbed the floor, making it ripple slightly. It took a moment to see it properly. Not floor. A film of water threading across the tiles. Dwight hissed and yanked his legs up on the desk before he'd finished processing what he'd seen — crouched, both hands white-knuckled on the edges — and the sound that came out of him was closer to a startled animal than a person. " No no nonono, David..." David turned, saw his face, followed his eyes. “Fuck...” He tried to stand, grip tight against the desk edge, only for his legs to fold like wet paper. Orela surged forward, catching him under one arm on reflex, nearly going down with him. He was heavier than he looked, all soaked muscle and bone and adrenaline backlash. "I've got it," He pulled his arm free, righting himself and stepping back from her, knees buckling slightly as he righted himself. “Said m’fine.” The water was there. A thin skin of it across the tile, barely a shimmer, running in from the hallway as quietly and patiently as everything else the building had done tonight. Dwight was already hunched in on himself, visibly shrinking from the puddle, a steady quiet stream of “not again” drifting on near hyperventilation as Leon rubbed small circles on his back. Panicking was not going to help things. “Hey. You’re okay. It’s not the basement. We can figure it out. We have time.” Dwight's knuckles were white on the desk edge, his breathing coming in shallow pulls that weren't quite keeping up with demand. His eyes had gone to the floor and stuck there, tracking the thin skin of water like it might lunge. "I know," he said. "I know, I just—" "I know," Leon kept his tone low, not following his gaze down. "We need to move." David's voice cut across the room, flat and certain. He was already looking at the door. "If it's still coming in, we don't have time to sit here." “Go where, exactly?” Jake snapped from the counter, "Windows won't break. I've been at this for twenty minutes. Whatever this glass is, it doesn't want to shatter. And we’ve struck out on the doors already." “Blocked like the stairs?” David asked. Jake and Leon shared a look. “Stairs?” “Ghostface blocked us in. Plugged up one of the stairwells with random crap. That’s why we had to go through the pipe hall. I think he’s still—” “Wait, he’s here?” Orela moved to hold David’s elbow again and only stepping back when he shot her a look full of steel and defiance. Dwight was trying to calm his breathing, to varying levels of success, redirecting his mind forcibly from the floor to literally anything else. “Didn’t you guys see him? He wasn’t even hiding when we came in. He was making a ton of noise." "We didn’t hear it," Jake looked down at the crowbar in his hand, thoughtful. "Actually, we've heard almost nothing this whole time. Building eats everything." Orela shook her head, confused. “There hasn’t been any kind of killer terror radius in here that we’ve felt. I had no idea he was even in this area. We had assumed whatever killer was assigned this trial got left outside.” “Besides,” Jake swung at the window one more time, crowbar bouncing harmlessly off, “The doors aren’t locked or blocked up. They’re jammed. The handles move fine, but the frame is swollen and warped so bad that the doors won’t budge.” Leon shared a meaningful glance with David and nodded. “That was when I was trying with Jake. With David, we have more muscle now. Between the three of us, we might be able to pry one of them open. What do you say? Feel up for a break and exit?” David looked at his shoulder. Rolled it once, deliberately. Took a couple steps, mentally logging the way his knees wobbled. The wince was small and controlled. He was steady enough for now. It would have to do. “Yeah. Ok. Let’s give it a go.” Orela swung her flashlight toward the hallway. The beam sliced the dark like a knife, catching on dust and soaked linoleum. “Let’s get out of here before the place decides we’re not interesting enough to keep.” In the hush that followed, Dwight kept his eyes on the floor. The water had reached the back wall. A thin layer, barely enough to splash — but moving. It was seeping in, quietly, purposefully. A slow reclaiming. Behind them, the walls pulsed. Just slightly.
